The Second Great Awakening spread the idea that people could perfect themselves and their society, while the market revolution brought factories, canals and growing cities with new problems like poverty and crime. At the same time, Jacksonian democracy had expanded voting rights for white men, which made the gap between American ideals and American reality harder to ignore.

Between 1820 and 1860, reform movements largely sought to expand democratic ideals by applying the promise of equality to groups that had been left out, especially enslaved people and women, though some reformers focused more on moral improvement and social order than on democracy itself.

Abolitionists made the strongest demand for equality. Garrison promised to fight for the "immediate enfranchisement of our slave population" and refused to speak with moderation (Doc 2). Because Garrison was writing in the first issue of his own newspaper, his purpose was to announce that the Liberator would not compromise, which explains his harsh tone. Frederick Douglass made a similar argument when he called American liberty a "sham" for enslaved people (Doc 7). As a formerly enslaved man speaking at a Fourth of July event, Douglass used the holiday to show his white audience how hollow their celebration of freedom was. asylum reform aimed at improving society as a whole.

Reform movements between 1820 and 1860 only partly expanded democratic ideals. Abolitionists and women's rights activists demanded that liberty and equality apply to everyone, but reformers of schools and asylums mostly tried to make society more orderly, and even radical reformers often disagreed about how far democracy should reach.
